claim: RAS proteins translate into four proteins: HRAS, NRAS, KRAS4A, and KRAS4B.
source: The RAS gene family translates into four proteins, namely HRAS, NRAS, KRAS4A, and KRAS4B, that control mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), and Ras-like (RAL) pathways (Barbacid, 1987; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2003; Lu et al., 2016a; Khan et al., 2019; Duffy and Crown, 2021; Simanshu et al., 2017; Ferro and Trabalzini, 2010; De Luca et al., 2012; Young et al., 2013; Knight and Irving, 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: RAS proteins control MAPK, PI3K, and RAL pathways.
source: The RAS gene family translates into four proteins, namely HRAS, NRAS, KRAS4A, and KRAS4B, that control mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), and Ras-like (RAL) pathways (Barbacid, 1987; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2003; Lu et al., 2016a; Khan et al., 2019; Duffy and Crown, 2021; Simanshu et al., 2017; Ferro and Trabalzini, 2010; De Luca et al., 2012; Young et al., 2013; Knight and Irving, 2014).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: RAS proteins act as a binary switch modulated by GTP and GDP.
source: These small G proteins act as a binary switch as the activation of the protein is modulated by two types of nucleotides, namely, guanosine-triphosphate (GTP) and guanosine-diphosphate (GDP).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and reflects established knowledge about RAS protein function.

claim: The exchange of GDP for GTP is maintained by guanine exchange factors (GEFs).
source: The exchange of GDP for GTP is maintained by guanine exchange factors (GEFs) which, in turn, activates the RAS protein (Downward, 1990; Grand and Owen, 1991; Bourne et al., 1991; Wittinghofer and Pai, 1991; Lowy et al., 1991; Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011; Takai et al., 2001; Lamontanara et al., 2014; Vetter and Wittinghofer, 2001; Lu et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Activated RAS proteins can interact with their downstream effectors, initiating cellular signaling pathways.
source: Consequently, activated RAS proteins can interact with their downstream effectors, thus initiating cellular signaling pathways (Vetter and Wittinghofer, 2001; Cherfils and Zeghouf, 2013; Geyer and Wittinghofer, 1997; Lu et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: GAPs accelerate the intrinsic GTPase activity of RAS.
source: Unlike GEFs, GTPase-activating-proteins (GAPs) accelerate the intrinsic GTPase activity of RAS, which provides a control mechanism for precise termination of respective signaling pathways (Wittinghofer et al., 1997; Lu et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: RAS proteins are made up of the G domain (residues 1–172) and hypervariable region (173–188 or –189).
source: RAS proteins are made up of two domains, namely, G domain (residues 1–172) and hypervariable region (173–188 or –189) (O'Bryan, 2019; Khan et al., 2020, Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and references Figure 1A for visual support, with citations provided.

claim: The G domain consists of effector lobe (residues 1–86) and allosteric lobe (residues 87–172).
source: The G domain consists of effector (residues 1–86) and allosteric lobes (residues 87–172).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The effector lobe harbors the P-loop (residues 10–17), Switch I (30-38), and Switch II (59-76) regions.
source: The former, which is the invariant region, harbors the P-loop (residues 10–17), Switch I (30-38), and Switch II (59-76) regions, the last two of which adopt different conformational states depending on the type of the nucleotide (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Switch I/II adopt different conformational states depending on the type of nucleotide.
source: The former, which is the invariant region, harbors the P-loop (residues 10–17), Switch I (30-38), and Switch II (59-76) regions, the last two of which adopt different conformational states depending on the type of the nucleotide (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Switch I/II can be found in either open or closed conformation.
source: In particular, Switch I/II can be found in either open or closed conformation, both of which are described depending on the position of the domain with respect to the nucleotide-binding pocket.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: In the open conformation, Switch I/II is far from the nucleotide-binding pocket and prevents effector binding.
source: In the open conformation, Switch I/II is far from the nucleotide-binding pocket, whereas it is closer in the closed conformation. Importantly, the former prevents effector binding while the latter favors it.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: In the closed conformation, Switch I/II is closer to the nucleotide-binding pocket and favors effector binding.
source: In the open conformation, Switch I/II is far from the nucleotide-binding pocket, whereas it is closer in the closed conformation. Importantly, the former prevents effector binding while the latter favors it.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Switch II becomes less stable upon effector binding.
source: Moreover, it has been also shown that Switch II becomes less stable upon effector binding, which presumably allows RAS to cycle between catalytically incompetent and competent states in a timely manner that is important for maintaining the cell homeostasis (Johnson and Mattos, 2013; Khan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: RAS mutations are frequently found at the 12th, 13th, and 61st residues.
source: Since RAS proteins are involved in signaling pathways, which are responsible for cell growth, differentiation, and proliferation, mutations, which are frequently found at the 12th, 13th, and 61st residues (Prior et al., 2020; Prior et al., 2012, cause several cancer types Holderfield et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2014; Prior et al., 2012; Stephen et al., 2014; McCormick, 2015a; McCormick, 2015b; Krens et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2016a as a result of attenuated GTP hydrolysis and increased nucleotide exchange rate Vigil et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: RAS mutations cause several cancer types as a result of attenuated GTP hydrolysis and increased nucleotide exchange rate.
source: Since RAS proteins are involved in signaling pathways, which are responsible for cell growth, differentiation, and proliferation, mutations, which are frequently found at the 12th, 13th, and 61st residues (Prior et al., 2020; Prior et al., 2012, cause several cancer types Holderfield et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2014; Prior et al., 2012; Stephen et al., 2014; McCormick, 2015a; McCormick, 2015b; Krens et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2016a as a result of attenuated GTP hydrolysis and increased nucleotide exchange rate Vigil et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: HRASG12D is the dominant mutant in ductal carcinoma.
source: For instance, HRASG12D was shown to be the dominant mutant in ductal carcinoma (Myers et al., 2016) caused resistance to erlotinib, which is used as an epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (Hah et al., 2014), in head and neck squamous carcinoma.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: HRASG12D caused resistance to erlotinib in head and neck squamous carcinoma.
source: For instance, HRASG12D was shown to be the dominant mutant in ductal carcinoma (Myers et al., 2016) caused resistance to erlotinib, which is used as an epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (Hah et al., 2014), in head and neck squamous carcinoma.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: No RAS inhibitors have yet been approved for clinical use.

claim: The GTP-bound state of mutants has been targeted except for KRASG12C mutant.
source: Also, except KRASG12C mutant, the GTP-bound state of mutants has been targeted as they either lose their intrinsic or GAP-mediated GTPase activity.

claim: The intrinsic GTPase activity of KRASG12C is relatively higher than other mutants, enabling targeting in its GDP-bound state.

claim: The undruggability of RAS proteins arises from lack of deep binding pockets on the surface of the protein and picomolar affinity of endogenous ligands.
source: The undruggability of RAS proteins arises from lack of deep binding pockets on the surface of the protein and also picomolar affinity of the endogenous ligands which hinders development of competitive inhibitors (Gysin et al., 2011; Ledford, 2015; Cox et al., 2014; Milroy and Ottmann, 2014).

claim: Phosphorylation of tyrosine at the 32nd position by Src-kinase attenuated RAF binding to HRAS and NRAS.
source: It has been shown that phosphorylation of the tyrosine at the 32nd position by Src-kinase attenuated RAF binding to HRAS and NRAS while elevating intrinsic GTPase activity of the proteins (Bunda et al., 2014, Figure 1B).

claim: Phosphorylation of tyrosine at the 32nd position by Src-kinase elevated intrinsic GTPase activity of HRAS and NRAS.
source: It has been shown that phosphorylation of the tyrosine at the 32nd position by Src-kinase attenuated RAF binding to HRAS and NRAS while elevating intrinsic GTPase activity of the proteins (Bunda et al., 2014, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated, supported by a citation, and references Figure 1B.

claim: Src-kinase phosphorylated tyrosine residues at the 32nd and 64th positions of KRAS4B isoform changed conformation of Switch I and II.
source: Furthermore, recently, Kano et al. have implied that Src-kinase phosphorylated tyrosine residues at the 32nd and 64th positions of KRAS4B isoform changed conformation of Switch I and II.

claim: Deletion or inhibition of SHP2 could slow down tumor progression but is insufficient for tumor regression.

claim: Phosphorylation increased the flexibility of Y32 as a result of repulsion between negatively charged phosphate and GTP.

claim: Phosphorylation did not impact the RAF-CRD interface.

claim: Phosphorylation pushed Switch I out of the binding pocket.
source: We showed that phosphorylation pushed Switch I out of the binding pocket as the distance between G12 and P34 residues increased compared to the mutant protein (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).

claim: Phosphorylation makes the nucleotide-binding pocket more accessible to waters.
source: Consequently, this makes the nucleotide-binding pocket more accessible to waters, as evident from the number of waters measured within 5 Å distance of GTP: 93.60±0.20, 100.30±0.20, and 72.68±0.17 for HRAS WT, HRASpY32, and HRASG12D,respectively.

claim: Y32 displayed two peaks at –100 to –90° and 80–90° in the phosphorylated RAS.
